subChunks.title: Publishing Family Histories & Genealogical Journals

storyBeats.txt: Research that is never published is research that never happened — at least, not for anyone else, Theodora said. The written record is what persists. The conversation you had with your grandmother about her childhood will be lost when both of you are gone, unless someone wrote it down and kept it.

Publishing family history is an act of preservation as much as an act of scholarship. A properly documented family narrative, with cited sources and accurate pedigrees, will still be useful to a researcher a century from now. An unsourced family legend will be an obstacle — plausible enough to mislead, unreliable enough to corrupt.

The standards for published genealogical work are not optional just because your audience is a family rather than an academic journal. If anything, the obligation is higher — family members are less likely to have the critical skills to detect errors, and those errors will propagate.

subChunks.hookHtml:
Family history publishing has been transformed by digital technology. What once required a commercial printer now requires only a laptop. Print-on-demand services mean a single copy or a thousand can be produced for the same unit cost. Websites, blogs, and digital archives allow families scattered across the world to access research in real time. The barriers to publishing have fallen dramatically.

But the standards have not fallen with them. A family history published without source citations, full of unsourced claims, errors in pedigrees, and identifiable living people whose privacy has not been protected is worse than no family history — it becomes the source from which the next generation's errors will propagate. Understanding the standards for published genealogical work, the formats available, and the ethical obligations of publication is essential for any professional genealogist.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Formats for Published Family History

Published family histories take many forms:

  • Narrative family history: A prose narrative following the family's story across generations, combining historical context with genealogical fact. The most readable format; the most demanding to write well. Suitable for family audiences.
  • Register system: A formal genealogical report format using a standardised numbering system (Register or NGSQ format) to record all descendants of a specific ancestor. Highly systematic and searchable; less narrative but more comprehensive. Used in society journals for published lineage studies.
  • Ahnentafel: A numbered pedigree format ascending through all direct ancestors of one individual. Each person has a number; the subject is 1; parents are 2 (father) and 3 (mother); grandparents 4–7, etc. Compact and systematic; not narrative.
  • Database/website format: Family trees published on platforms (Ancestry, WikiTree, Genealobank) or personal websites. Most accessible; requires careful attention to privacy (living people) and citation standards.
  • Journal article: A peer-reviewed article in a genealogical journal, typically presenting a proof argument or a documented lineage study. The highest-prestige form of genealogical publication.

The Register System

The Register format (New England Register, developed by the New England Historic Genealogical Society) assigns Arabic numerals to all children; those who appear later as parents receive a superscripted Roman numeral. The NGSQ format (National Genealogical Society Quarterly) uses a similar numbering. Both allow the reader to follow any line of descent through the publication.

For a published lineage study in a journal, the Register or NGSQ format is standard. Learning these formats is essential for professional genealogists who intend to publish descendant studies.

Citation Standards in Published Work

Published family histories must meet the same citation standards as professional research reports — more so, since published work will be used by researchers who cannot ask the author for clarification. Every factual assertion about an ancestor's birth, marriage, death, occupation, or location requires a cited source. Undocumented family traditions must be clearly labelled as such. Inconsistencies must be acknowledged.

The challenge of citation in narrative prose: citations must not interrupt the narrative to the point of unreadability, but must be sufficient to enable verification. The standard solution: endnotes (grouped at the back of the book or chapter) for published family histories, footnotes for journal articles. Full Evidence Explained citations in endnotes; shorter references in the text.

Privacy in Published Family Histories

Standard practice: living individuals are not included by name in published family histories. Spouses, children, and other relatives who are living should be referred to as 'living' or '[name withheld]'. Only deceased individuals are identified by name. This principle applies whether the publication is print or online.

For digital/online publication: platform privacy settings must be used correctly. Ancestry, WikiTree, and Geni all have provisions for marking individuals as living; ensure these are activated. Be aware that even if an individual is marked 'living' in the tree, other information (physical documents, photographs) uploaded alongside may reveal identifying information.

Print-on-Demand and Self-Publishing

Major print-on-demand platforms for family histories: Lulu.com, Amazon KDP (Kindle Direct Publishing), IngramSpark, Blurb. Each provides: online book design tools; hardcover and softcover options; single-copy printing; and (for wider distribution) ISBN provision and distribution through bookshops. Costs per copy are higher than offset printing but there is no minimum order — a family history can be printed in runs of 10–20 copies for family distribution without the minimum order constraints of traditional printing.

For the most important family history documents, consider also depositing a copy with the relevant county local studies library, the Society of Genealogists library, or a national library. This provides institutional preservation independent of any individual or family's care.

Genealogical Journal Publication

The peer-reviewed genealogical journals — NGSQ, The Genealogist, The New England Ancestor, county society journals — publish original research articles (typically documented lineage studies or proof arguments). Submission guidelines vary; most follow the NGSQ style sheet, which is publicly available. Submission requires following the house style for citations, the Register format for lineages, and the standard GPS framework for analytical articles.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why a family history published online with no source citations is worse than not publishing at all — and what standards a properly published family history should meet.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: You have completed a three-generation family history of the Walker family of Yorkshire, covering six individuals born between 1780 and 1890. You want to make it available to family members and deposit a copy with the local studies library. Outline: (1) the format you would choose for publication; (2) how you would handle two living individuals (a great-great-grandson born 1948 and a great-great-granddaughter born 1952) who appear at the end of your pedigree; (3) three specific citation practices you would apply throughout; and (4) the print-on-demand platform you would use and why.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Format: A narrative family history with an ahnentafel appendix for systematic reference. The narrative provides readability for family members; the ahnentafel provides a systematic pedigree that can be cross-referenced. Endnotes (not footnotes) for citations to avoid disrupting the prose narrative.

(2) Living individuals: The great-great-grandson (b. 1948) and great-great-granddaughter (b. 1952) would appear in the printed publication as '[Name withheld, born 1948]' and '[Name withheld, born 1952]' respectively. Their inclusion shows the family's continuity without identifying living people by name. If they have given explicit written consent to be named, they can be named — but the default is anonymisation. Any children or grandchildren of these individuals would be omitted entirely.

(3) Citation practices: (a) Every birth/marriage/death fact cited with the specific GRO registration reference or parish register entry. (b) Census facts cited with the full piece/folio/page reference and the digital platform and access date. (c) Family tradition claims labelled explicitly as unverified oral tradition rather than documented fact, with a note of who provided the information and when it was recorded.

(4) Print-on-demand: Lulu.com or IngramSpark — both produce good-quality hardcover books with no minimum order, allowing 15–20 copies for family distribution plus one for the library deposit. A formal ISBN is advisable for library deposit (both platforms provide this for a small fee), as it enables the library to catalogue and locate the item correctly in future.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: You are preparing a narrative family history for publication. One section describes your client's ancestor, who was a British colonial official in early 20th century Nigeria. You have found documentary evidence of his administrative work, personal letters he wrote home describing local people in terms that reflect the racist language of his era, and a photograph of him with local officials. How would you handle: (1) the use of racist language from primary sources; (2) the photograph; (3) the overall framing of this section, given that your client is proud of this ancestor's service?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Racist language from primary sources: The letters are original, primary sources documenting the ancestor's attitudes and actions. They cannot be altered. However, they can be handled with scholarly care: quote directly but introduce the quotation with appropriate contextualisation ('In a letter reflecting the common racial attitudes of British colonial administrators of this period, he wrote...'); do not reproduce gratuitously offensive language beyond what is necessary to document his views and actions; explain in the narrative that such language was standard in colonial administration and reflects systemic attitudes, not merely individual prejudice. The alternative — paraphrasing or omitting the quotations — would sanitise the historical record.

(2) The photograph: Include it, with a careful caption. The photograph is a historical document recording a specific administrative encounter. The local officials depicted in it are historical persons with their own dignity and historical significance. Caption the photograph with as much information as you can establish about who they are and the context of the image — not just the ancestor's name. Avoid using the image to illustrate anything other than its specific historical content.

(3) Framing: The narrative should present the evidence honestly, including the aspects your client finds uncomfortable. It is appropriate to explain that the ancestor's career achievements within the colonial administration were real and significant within that context — and that the colonial administration itself was a system whose historical consequences for Nigeria were profound and contested. The client's pride in his ancestor's 'service' can be acknowledged alongside the complexity of what that service meant. This is not editorialising — it is historical context. A family history that presents only the ancestor's perspective on their own work is incomplete.
learningObjectives: Describe the principal formats for published family history (narrative, Register system, ahnentafel, database, journal article) and their appropriate use cases.
Apply citation standards, privacy protections, and honest treatment of family traditions to a published family history.
Use print-on-demand platforms to publish a family history for family distribution and library deposit.
Explain the ethical obligations in presenting difficult historical material in a published family history.
commonMistakes: Publishing a family history with insufficient citations — published work will be used by future researchers who cannot ask the author for verification.
Including living individuals by name in print or online publications without explicit consent.
Presenting unverified family traditions as documented fact rather than labelling them clearly as oral tradition.
Sanitising the historical record by omitting or softening difficult findings to protect a family's self-image.
assessmentCriteria: Selects an appropriate publication format for the stated audience and purpose.
Correctly applies the living-person privacy standard, using 'name withheld' or 'living' designations.
Demonstrates Evidence Explained-standard citation practice throughout.
Handles difficult historical material with scholarly honesty and appropriate contextualisation.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Standardised genealogical publication formats using numbered entries for systematic descendant studies; used by peer-reviewed genealogical journals for lineage articles.

A numbered pedigree system for direct ancestors; the subject is number 1, father 2, mother 3, paternal grandparents 4–5, maternal grandparents 6–7 — allowing compact, systematic pedigree presentation.
Publishing model that produces copies to order with no minimum print run; major genealogical publishing platforms include Lulu.com, IngramSpark, and Amazon KDP.
The UK's largest genealogical library (London); accepts deposits of published family histories and genealogical research for preservation and public access.

The house style guidelines of the National Genealogical Society Quarterly, covering citation format, Register system numbering, and article structure — the de facto standard for genealogical journal publication.

questions.questionHtml: In the ahnentafel numbering system, what number is assigned to the subject's paternal grandfather?
questions.explanationHtml: In the ahnentafel system: subject = 1; father = 2; mother = 3; paternal grandfather = 4; paternal grandmother = 5; maternal grandfather = 6; maternal grandmother = 7. The pattern is that each person's father is 2n and mother is 2n+1 where n is that person's number.

questions.questionHtml: You are writing a narrative family history chapter and need to reference a living cousin (born 1965) who appears in the family tree. How should you handle this in the published text?
options: Use their full name since it is a family publication and family members know each other
Refer to them as '[Name withheld, born 1965]' or 'living' — standard privacy practice for living individuals in published family histories
Omit them entirely since living people cannot appear in family histories
questions.correctAnswer: Refer to them as '[Name withheld, born 1965]' or 'living' — standard privacy practice for living individuals in published family histories
questions.explanationHtml: Standard practice in published family histories protects living individuals by withholding their names, even in family-circulated publications. The birth year provides genealogical context while preserving privacy. This standard applies regardless of whether the subject knows they are included.

questions.questionHtml: A client asks you to write a family history narrative but says: 'Please don't include any of the criminal records you found — I don't want the family to know.' How should you respond?
options: Agree — the client is paying and it's their family history
Explain that omitting documented evidence produces a misleading account; offer to contextualise the findings sensitively within the historical narrative rather than omitting them
Include the criminal records prominently in the opening chapter to ensure they are not overlooked
Include them only if the client explicitly agrees to it in writing
questions.correctAnswer: Explain that omitting documented evidence produces a misleading account; offer to contextualise the findings sensitively within the historical narrative rather than omitting them
questions.explanationHtml: A family history that omits documented evidence on a client's request is not a history — it is a selective account. The genealogist's professional obligation to present evidence honestly applies to published work as well as research reports. Offering to contextualise sensitively is a constructive compromise; agreeing to suppress evidence entirely is not.
